prompt.context: Our client is Rotisserie Ranch, a poultry farming company that specializes in growing chickens for rotisserie roasting. Its primary customer segment is comprised of large grocery chains that buy its chickens to fresh roast in the meat departments of their grocery stores. Market research has revealed to Rotisserie Ranch that more and more consumers have begun buying flavored rotisserie chickens recently.
prompt.question: Rotisserie Ranch is thinking of pre-flavoring some of its chickens for grocers. What would you consider in making this recommendation?

clarifying_info.a: Predicting demand for cooked chickens is difficult for grocers; any leftover cooked chickens at the end of the day are thrown out; unthawed chickens cannot be re-frozen.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have any competitive advantage in this space?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a patented process for sterilely packaging chicken so that it will remain fresh for 30 days, making freezing unnecessary.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current market position?
clarifying_info.a: The client is currently the industry market share leader in rotisserie-ready chicken.
Four new flavored products to be introduced concurrently: Barbecue, lemon herb, tandoori, and teriyaki.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors in this new product space?
clarifying_info.a: For this case, assume Rotisserie Ranch will only compete against existing Private Label brands at grocery stores. No competition in the new product market due to the patented process — competitors freeze chicken and therefore cannot pre-season it.

exhibits.title: Store Sales — Standard vs. BBQ Seasoned Rotisserie
exhibits.shows: A table comparing weekly sales data for two Standard Rotisserie stores (A and B) and two BBQ Seasoned Rotisserie test-market stores (C and D), showing weekly sales revenue, retail price per chicken, and retailer margin for each store.

framework: Value to customers (grocery chains) — will they buy the pre-seasoned product?
Revenue and cost implications of new venture for both Rotisserie Ranch and its grocer customers
Cost increase to client must be offset by price increase to grocers
Competitive dynamics — who else offers pre-seasoned rotisserie chicken and can they replicate it?

questions.prompt: Prompt 1: Do you think that grocery retailers would be interested in pre-seasoned chickens from Rotisserie Ranch?
questions.guidance: No single correct answer; evaluate quality of reasoning. A strong YES answer covers: (1) Labor Cost Reduction — meat department workers no longer spend time seasoning; (2) Economies of Scale — centralized seasoning lowers cost; (3) Product Consistency — centrally managed R&D produces more reliable flavor. A strong NO answer covers: (1) Loss of Differentiation — grocery chains differentiate by value-added in-store; (2) Local Taste Attunement — grocers may be better at gauging local consumer preferences; (3) Increases Inventory and SKUs, adding operational complexity.

questions.prompt: Prompt 2: After several interviews, grocers are interested in Rotisserie Ranch's proposed new product, but first they want to be sure the chickens will sell well. How would you make sure?
questions.guidance: The correct answer is to run a test market for the new products. Key points: (1) A pilot test should be run before full rollout; (2) The pilot needs a control or comparison group (e.g., stores selling standard chicken vs. stores selling seasoned chicken) so results are meaningful. Candidate may elaborate on test design — cut off once it is clear they understand pilot + control group.

questions.prompt: Prompt 3: A test market launch for the new Rotisserie Ranch BBQ chicken was administered (hand interviewee Exhibit 1). What is the overall profit for both Store A and Store B, and for both Store C and Store D, from the test market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate retailer profit (weekly sales × retailer margin) for each store and then compare totals across standard vs. seasoned product. Key insight: even though the retailer margin percentage is lower for seasoned chicken (25% vs. 30%), higher weekly sales revenue drives higher absolute profit for grocers.

math.setup: Retailer profit = Weekly Sales × Retailer Margin. Compare total profit across Standard Rotisserie stores (A+B) vs. BBQ Seasoned Rotisserie stores (C+D).
steps: Incremental profit for grocers from seasoned chicken: $1,075 − $900 = $175/week
math.answer: Standard stores earn $900/week total; BBQ Seasoned stores earn $1,075/week total — an increase of $175/week in gross profit for grocery retailers.

recommendation: Rotisserie Ranch should launch the Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken product and use results to test and expand to additional flavors (lemon herb, tandoori, teriyaki).
risks: If test market stores were not representative, results may not generalize to full rollout.
Lower retailer margin percentage (25% vs. 30%) could create friction in negotiations if weekly sales volumes underperform test levels.
Operational complexity of managing four flavors concurrently and perishability logistics.
next_steps: Confirm test market representativeness and scale findings to full grocer network.
Negotiate pricing and margin structure with grocery chain partners for each flavor.
Monitor sell-through rates closely post-launch to manage perishability and minimize waste.
Evaluate scale benefits to Rotisserie Ranch's own cost structure as seasoned chicken volume grows.
